title: Introduction to Trigonometry
summary: This chapter builds the entire trigonometry toolkit of Class 10. It begins with the six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle of a right triangle, defined as fixed ratios of the perpendicular, base and hypotenuse, and explains why these ratios depend only on the angle and not on the size of the triangle. Exact values of all six ratios are tabulated for the standard angles 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees and are then used to evaluate compound expressions quickly and exactly. The three fundamental identities sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A and 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A are derived from the Pythagoras theorem and applied to prove harder identities, usually by converting every ratio into sin and cos. The chapter closes with the ratios of complementary angles, such as sin (90 - A) = cos A, which power classics like tan 1 tan 2 ... tan 89 = 1 and angle-finding equations built on standard angles.
hotTopics: Naming perpendicular, base and hypotenuse for a chosen acute angle
The six trigonometric ratios and their reciprocal pairs
Exact values of ratios for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees
Evaluating compound expressions using the standard table
Proof of sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 from the Pythagoras theorem
The identities 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A and 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A
Proving identities by converting everything into sin and cos
Ratios of complementary angles and the swap pairs
Finding all six ratios from one given ratio
Reading standard angles from equations like sin (A + B) = 1

sections.heading: Why Trigonometry and the Language of Right Triangles
sections.para: Trigonometry was invented to answer questions no ruler could reach: the height of a pyramid, the width of a river, the distance of a ship from the shore. The word itself means measurement of triangles, and Class 10 confines the study to right triangles, where one angle is exactly 90 degrees. Everything in this chapter flows from one picture: a right triangle with an acute angle marked, its opposite side named the perpendicular, its other adjacent side named the base, and the longest side, opposite the right angle, named the hypotenuse. Once the sides are named with respect to a chosen angle, the six ratios become unavoidable vocabulary. Mastering this naming step is therefore the real first lesson of trigonometry, because a wrongly named side silently destroys every ratio and every answer written after it.
points: Trigonometry studies relationships between the angles and the sides of triangles; in this chapter only right triangles with one 90 degree angle are used.

For an acute angle A in right triangle ABC right angled at B, the side BC opposite A is the perpendicular, the side AB adjacent to A is the base, and the side AC opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse.
The names perpendicular and base change when the reference angle changes: for angle C of the same triangle, AB becomes the perpendicular and BC becomes the base.
The hypotenuse is always the longest side and never changes its name because it is fixed opposite the 90 degree angle.
The values of the ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle, because all right triangles with the same acute angle are similar to each other.
The word trigonometry comes from Greek words meaning three angles measure, and the subject grew out of astronomy and land surveying.
Every question in this chapter and in heights and distances begins with a rough labelled sketch; drawing it is not decoration but the actual method of solution.
In symbols, sin A is read as sine of angle A and is one indivisible symbol; it never means the number sin multiplied by the number A.

keyTerms.meaning: A triangle with one angle exactly 90 degrees; the only triangle used to define Class 10 trigonometric ratios.
The longest side of a right triangle, always opposite the 90 degree angle.
The side opposite the chosen acute angle; also called the opposite side.
The side adjacent to the chosen acute angle other than the hypotenuse; also called the adjacent side.
The particular acute angle with respect to which the sides are being named and the ratios computed.
Triangles with equal corresponding angles; the reason ratios are the same for every right triangle containing a given acute angle.

sections.trick: Name the sides looking FROM the chosen angle: the side facing the angle is the perpendicular, the side the angle sits on is the base, and the side facing the right angle is the hypotenuse.
sections.examPointer: Correct labelling of a right triangle is quietly tested inside every 2 to 3 mark definition question and inside every proof; one mislabelled side zeroes out all the ratios that follow.

sections.heading: The Six Trigonometric Ratios
sections.para: For a chosen acute angle A of a right triangle, the six trigonometric ratios are three primary ratios and their three reciprocals. The primary ratios are sin A = perpendicular/hypotenuse, cos A = base/hypotenuse and tan A = perpendicular/base, remembered by the sentence SOH CAH TOA. Their reciprocals are cosec A = hypotenuse/perpendicular, sec A = hypotenuse/base and cot A = base/perpendicular. Two extra links are worth memorising: tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A, which follow directly by dividing the definitions. Each ratio is a pure number with no units, because it is a ratio of two lengths measured in the same unit. The ratios are defined only for acute angles of right triangles at this level, and tan A and sec A fail at 90 degrees while sin A and cos A never fail in the range 0 to 90 degrees.
points: Primary ratios: sin A = perpendicular/hypotenuse, cos A = base/hypotenuse, tan A = perpendicular/base.
Reciprocal ratios: cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A; in side form, cosec A = hypotenuse/perpendicular, sec A = hypotenuse/base, cot A = base/perpendicular.
Quotient links: tan A = sin A/cos A and cot A = cos A/sin A, valid whenever cos A and sin A respectively are not zero.
Worked mini-example: if perpendicular = 3, base = 4 and hypotenuse = 5, then sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4 and cot A = 4/3.
Each ratio is a number without units because it compares two lengths in the same unit.
Common error: writing cosec A = 1/cos A; the correct partner of cosec is sin, and the correct partner of sec is cos.
Common error: treating sin^2 A as sin A^2; the notation sin^2 A always means (sin A)^2, the square of the value of the ratio.
Range facts used constantly: 0 is less than or equal to sin A and cos A, which are less than or equal to 1 for 0 to 90 degrees, while tan A can take any non-negative value.

keyTerms.meaning: Ratio perpendicular/hypotenuse for angle A; read as sine of angle A.
Ratio base/hypotenuse for angle A; read as cosine of angle A.
Ratio perpendicular/base, equal to sin A/cos A; undefined when cos A = 0, that is at 90 degrees.
Reciprocal of sin A, equal to hypotenuse/perpendicular; undefined when sin A = 0, that is at 0 degrees.
Reciprocal of cos A, equal to hypotenuse/base; undefined at 90 degrees.
Reciprocal of tan A and equal to cos A/sin A; undefined at 0 degrees and equal to 0 at 90 degrees.

sections.trick: SOH CAH TOA gives the big three: Sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite/Adjacent; then flip each ratio upside down to get cosec, sec and cot.
sections.examPointer: Writing all six ratios from a labelled triangle or from one given ratio is a standing 2 to 3 mark question, and the reciprocal pairings cosec-sin and sec-cos are the most common careless slips.

sections.heading: Exact Values for 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 Degrees
sections.para: The standard angle table is the multiplication table of trigonometry: it must be instant recall, not derived during the exam. For 45 degrees, an isosceles right triangle with equal legs 1 gives hypotenuse sqrt(2), so sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2) and tan 45 = 1. For 30 and 60 degrees, drop the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side 2; the halves have sides 1, sqrt(3) and 2, giving sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2 and tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3), with the 60 degree values read from the other acute angle. The sine column is sqrt(0)/2, sqrt(1)/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(4)/2 as the angle walks 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees, and cos is the same list read backwards. Tan equals sin divided by cos, so tan 90 is not defined because cos 90 = 0 appears in the denominator.
points: 45 degrees comes from the isosceles right triangle with legs 1: sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)/2 and tan 45 = 1.
30 and 60 degrees come from the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side 2, producing the triple 1, sqrt(3), 2.
Values: sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3); sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 60 = sqrt(3).
End values: sin 0 = 0, cos 0 = 1, tan 0 = 0; sin 90 = 1, cos 90 = 0, cot 90 = 0, and tan 90 and sec 90 are not defined.
Reciprocal highlights: cosec 30 = 2, sec 60 = 2, cosec 0 is not defined, sec 0 = 1, cosec 90 = 1, cot 45 = 1.
Memory trick: the sine values are sqrt(0)/2, sqrt(1)/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(4)/2 for angles 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees; cos is the reverse order and tan = sin/cos.
Rationalise at the end if needed: 1/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)/2 and 1/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3)/3, but keep surd forms during working.
Common error: quoting tan 90 = infinity; the correct statement is that tan 90 is not defined because cos 90 = 0.

keyTerms.meaning: The angles 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees whose exact ratio values are tabulated and memorised.
The status of tan 90 and sec 90, since cos 90 = 0 sits in the denominator; also of cosec 0 and cot 0 since sin 0 = 0.
Rewriting 1/sqrt(2) as sqrt(2)/2 or 1/sqrt(3) as sqrt(3)/3 to remove the surd from the denominator.
A surd or fraction such as sqrt(3)/2 that expresses the ratio precisely, preferred over a decimal in board answers.

sections.trick: Hold up one hand: sin of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 is sqrt of the fingers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 divided by 2; cos is the same hand counted from the other side, and tan is sin divided by cos.
sections.examPointer: One evaluation question built directly on this table appears in almost every paper; the 30, 45 and 60 degree columns must be recalled in under a minute, and tan 90 not defined is a favourite one-marker.

sections.heading: Evaluating Expressions with Standard Values
sections.para: Evaluation questions ask you to substitute exact table values into an expression and simplify to a single fraction. The reliable order of operations is: write the expression, replace every ratio by its exact value, keep squares as squares, simplify each term separately, then combine using one common denominator. For example, 5 sin^2 30 + cos^2 45 - 4 tan^2 30 = 5(1/2)^2 + (1/sqrt(2))^2 - 4(1/sqrt(3))^2 = 5/4 + 1/2 - 4/3 = (15 + 6 - 16)/12 = 5/12. Products of complementary pairs, such as sin 30 cos 60, simplify instantly because the two factors are equal. Rationalise only at the very end so that surds do not multiply into long chains mid-solution. A quick numerical check with approximate decimals catches most slips before the final answer is written.
points: Substitution rule: replace sin 30 by 1/2, cos 60 by 1/2, tan 45 by 1, tan 30 by 1/sqrt(3), and so on, before any other simplification.
Worked example: 5 sin^2 30 + cos^2 45 - 4 tan^2 30 = 5/4 + 1/2 - 4/3 = 5/12 using denominator 12.
Complementary shortcuts: sin 30 cos 60 + cos 30 sin 60 = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1 because sin 30 = cos 60 and cos 30 = sin 60.
Squares of unit-friendly values: sin^2 30 = 1/4, cos^2 60 = 1/4, tan^2 45 = 1, sin^2 60 = 3/4, cot^2 45 = 1.
Identities beat tables when an angle is unknown: 9 sec^2 A - 9 tan^2 A = 9(sec^2 A - tan^2 A) = 9 for every admissible angle A.
Common error: computing (sin 30)^2 as sin 30^2, that is squaring the 30 instead of the ratio 1/2; the angle is never squared.
Keep surds till the last step and rationalise once, at the end, to avoid messy intermediate fractions.
Final check: convert your fraction to a decimal mentally and compare with a rough decimal estimate of each term.

keyTerms.meaning: Replacing each trigonometric ratio by its exact standard value before simplifying.
The LCM of the denominators of the terms, used to add and subtract fractions cleanly.
Two ratios like sin 30 and cos 60 that are equal because the angles add to 90 degrees.
Reducing a trigonometric expression to a single exact number or fraction.

sections.trick: SUBSTITUTE, SQUARE, SEPARATE, SUM: put in table values, square them, simplify each term alone, then merge over one common denominator at the end.
sections.examPointer: A 2 mark evaluation like the 5/12 example above is near-guaranteed; full marks need the substitution line, the per-term values, and the final simplified fraction, not just the answer.

sections.heading: The Three Fundamental Identities and Their Proofs
sections.para: An identity is an equation true for every value of the angle for which both sides are defined. All three fundamental identities are shadows of one Pythagoras statement in a right triangle ABC right angled at B with acute angle A. Dividing AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2 by AC^2 gives (BC/AC)^2 + (AB/AC)^2 = 1, which is sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1. Dividing the same statement by AB^2 gives tan^2 A + 1 = sec^2 A, valid except at 90 degrees, and dividing by BC^2 gives 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A, valid except at 0 degrees. The most useful rearrangements are sin^2 A = 1 - cos^2 A, sec^2 A - tan^2 A = 1 and cosec^2 A - cot^2 A = 1. In any proof, naming the identity you used at each step is what earns the method marks.
points: First identity: sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, obtained by dividing the Pythagoras statement by the hypotenuse squared.
Second identity: 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A, obtained by dividing by the base squared; it fails only at 90 degrees where tan and sec are not defined.
Third identity: 1 + cot^2 A = cosec^2 A, obtained by dividing by the perpendicular squared; it fails only at 0 degrees where cot and cosec are not defined.
Rearrangements to memorise: cos^2 A = 1 - sin^2 A, sin^2 A = 1 - cos^2 A, sec^2 A - tan^2 A = 1, cosec^2 A - cot^2 A = 1, cosec^2 A - 1 = cot^2 A, sec^2 A - 1 = tan^2 A.
Quick numerical check of the first identity at 30 degrees: (1/2)^2 + (sqrt(3)/2)^2 = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1.
Instant consequence: for any k, k sec^2 A - k tan^2 A = k and k cosec^2 A - k cot^2 A = k, so 9 sec^2 A - 9 tan^2 A = 9.
Notation warning: sin^2 A means (sin A)^2, never sin(A^2); the square is on the value of the ratio.
In proofs, write the identity being used beside the line, for example using sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, because CBSE awards step marks for named identities.

keyTerms.meaning: An equation between trigonometric expressions that holds for every admissible value of the angle.
An angle at which every ratio appearing in the identity is defined, for example angles other than 90 degrees for the tan-sec identity.
The statement hypotenuse^2 = perpendicular^2 + base^2 in a right triangle; the single source of all three identities.
An algebraic version of an identity, such as cosec^2 A - 1 = cot^2 A, ready to be substituted mid-proof.

sections.trick: One Pythagoras, three identities: divide by hypotenuse^2 for the sin-cos pair, by base^2 for the tan-sec pair, by perpendicular^2 for the cot-cosec pair.
sections.examPointer: Stating and proving any one identity from the Pythagoras theorem is a standard 3 marker, and using the identities without naming them is the most common way students lose method marks.

sections.heading: A Systematic Method for Proving Identities
sections.para: Proof questions mark the difference between knowing the identities and being able to use them. The universal strategy is: choose the more complicated side, convert every ratio into sin and cos, apply the fundamental identities or plain algebra, and drive the expression toward the simpler side without ever touching the given equation as an equation to be solved. For example, sec A (1 - sin A)(sec A + tan A) = ((1 - sin A)(1 + sin A))/cos^2 A = (1 - sin^2 A)/cos^2 A = cos^2 A/cos^2 A = 1. When direct reduction stalls, reduce both sides separately to the same simplest expression, or prove that LHS minus RHS equals 0. Never square both sides as a first move, because it can introduce false steps; factorisation and the identity sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 achieve nearly everything at this level.
points: Step 1 of every proof: pick the heavier side, usually the one with more terms or mixed ratios.
Step 2: rewrite cosec, sec, tan and cot in terms of sin and cos, since every identity collapses to sin and cos eventually.
Step 3: create the pattern sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 by adding and subtracting, or by factoring, for example 1 - sin^2 A = cos^2 A.
Worked classic: sec A (1 - sin A)(sec A + tan A) = 1 because (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A) = 1 - sin^2 A = cos^2 A and sec A + tan A = (1 + sin A)/cos A.
Worked classic: (cosec A - sin A) = cos^2 A/sin A and (sec A - cos A) = sin^2 A/cos A, so their product is sin A cos A, which equals 1/(tan A + cot A).
If both sides are complicated, reduce each side independently to the same expression and present both reductions in the answer.
Verification habit: substitute A = 30 or 45 degrees numerically into both sides; equal numbers confirm the algebra before you submit.
Forbidden move: multiplying both sides of the supposed identity or cross-multiplying as if it were an equation to solve; work one side at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: Left hand side and right hand side of the identity; the proof reduces one or both to a common expression.
The standard first move of rewriting tan, cot, sec and cosec using their definitions.
Recognising patterns like 1 - sin^2 A = (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A) to trigger the fundamental identity.
Numerical substitution of a standard angle to sanity-check a completed proof.

sections.trick: SIN-COS FIRST, SIMPLIFY SECOND: the moment a proof looks stuck, replace every foreign ratio by sin and cos; almost every Class 10 identity dies within three lines after that.
sections.examPointer: One identity proof of 3 to 5 marks is virtually certain in the board paper; examiners award marks for the conversion line, each named identity application, and a clean concluding statement.

sections.heading: Ratios of Complementary Angles
sections.para: Two angles are complementary when their sum is 90 degrees, and in every right triangle the two acute angles are complementary partners. For the complementary angle (90 - A), the perpendicular and base of the same triangle exchange roles, so each ratio changes to its partner ratio: sin (90 - A) = cos A, cos (90 - A) = sin A, tan (90 - A) = cot A, cot (90 - A) = tan A, sec (90 - A) = cosec A and cosec (90 - A) = sec A. This swap converts unfamiliar angles into familiar ones: sin 20 becomes cos 70, sec 48 becomes cosec 42. It also produces famous cancellations: in tan 1 tan 2 ... tan 89, each pair tan k and tan (90 - k) multiplies to 1, so the entire product is 1. The brackets are part of the symbol, so sin (90 - A) is never sin 90 minus sin A.
points: Complementary angles are a pair whose sum is 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, or A and (90 - A).
Swap pairs: sin and cos exchange, tan and cot exchange, sec and cosec exchange when the angle is replaced by its complement.
Reason: in the same right triangle, the angle (90 - A) sees the perpendicular and base with their roles interchanged, so each ratio becomes its partner.
Instant examples: sin 25 = cos 65, cos 48 = sin 42, tan 60 = cot 30, sec 72 = cosec 18.
Classic evaluation: sin 20 cos 70 + cos 20 sin 70 = cos^2 70 + sin^2 70 = 1 after applying the swaps.
Classic product: tan 1 tan 2 ... tan 89 = 1, because tan k tan (90 - k) = tan k cot k = 1 for each of the 44 pairs.
Angle-finding: if sin (A + 20) = cos (A - 10), then (A + 20) + (A - 10) = 90, giving A = 40 degrees.
Warning: sin (90 - A) is one symbol for the sine of the whole angle (90 - A); it is not sin 90 - sin A, which would be 1 - sin A.

keyTerms.meaning: A pair of angles whose sum is 90 degrees.
The rule that replacing an angle by (90 - A) interchanges sin with cos, tan with cot and sec with cosec.
The co-ratio that a ratio turns into under complementing: the partner of sin is cos, of tan is cot, of sec is cosec.

sections.trick: CO-SWAP: putting co- in front signals a complement; sin to cos, tan to cot, sec to cosec, and the angle must be subtracted from 90 first.
sections.examPointer: MCQs like evaluate tan 1 tan 2 ... tan 89, and one-liners such as find A if sin (A + 20) = cos (A - 10), repeat almost every year and are worth 1 to 2 marks each.

sections.heading: Finding All Ratios from One Given Ratio
sections.para: A single given ratio completely determines a right triangle up to scale, so all other ratios follow. The method is to sketch a triangle, assign the numerator and denominator of the given ratio to the correct sides, compute the third side by the Pythagoras theorem, and read off the remaining five ratios. For example, if tan A = 3/4, take perpendicular 3 and base 4, so the hypotenuse is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, giving sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4 and cot A = 4/3. If instead an identity-friendly value appears, such as sin A = 1/2, recognising the standard angle A = 30 degrees is faster than drawing. When the ratio involves a variable, like sin A = x, the Pythagoras step gives the third side as a surd in x, and the other ratios follow symbolically.
points: Method: from the given ratio fix two sides, get the third by hypotenuse^2 = perpendicular^2 + base^2, then write the other five ratios.
Worked example: tan A = 5/12 gives perpendicular 5, base 12, hypotenuse 13, so sin A = 5/13, cos A = 12/13, cosec A = 13/5, sec A = 13/12, cot A = 12/5.
Worked example: sec A = 13/5 gives hypotenuse 13, base 5, perpendicular 12, so tan A = 12/5 and sin A = 12/13.
Standard angle recognition: sin A = 1/2 means A = 30 degrees, tan A = 1 means A = 45 degrees, cos A = 1/2 means A = 60 degrees.
Algebraic case: if sin A = x, then cos A = sqrt(1 - x^2) and tan A = x/sqrt(1 - x^2), using sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1.
Useful identity route: (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A) = 1 - sin^2 A = cos^2 A, so a product question can be answered without finding A.
Common error: attaching the numerator of the given ratio to the wrong side; tan A = 3/4 means perpendicular 3 with base 4, not the other way.
Keep Pythagorean triples ready: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 9-40-41 and their multiples.

keyTerms.meaning: A set of positive integers like 3, 4, 5 that forms the sides of a right triangle, letting ratios be read instantly.
The fact that multiplying all sides by the same number leaves every trigonometric ratio unchanged.
An exact answer containing a root, such as sqrt(1 - x^2), kept unexpanded for precision.

sections.trick: One ratio paints the whole triangle: read the two legs from the fraction, Pythagoras the third side, then harvest the remaining five ratios in one glance.
sections.examPointer: Given one ratio, find the rest and evaluate a related expression: this combination is a repeated 2 to 3 mark question, and triples like 5-12-13 appear more often than any other.

sections.heading: Reading Standard Angles from Trigonometric Equations
sections.para: Many questions hide a standard angle inside an equation, and the skill is to translate each trigonometric fact into its angle and then solve the resulting linear conditions. Since sin (A + B) = 1 forces A + B = 90 degrees, sin (A - B) = 1/2 forces A - B = 30 degrees, and tan (A + B) = sqrt(3) forces A + B = 60 degrees, pairs of such conditions reduce to simultaneous linear equations in A and B. Restrictions matter: the given range such as 0 degrees less than B less than or equal to A less than 90 degrees picks the unique standard angle from the table. The same idea handles single equations like 2 sin A = 1 or tan (A + 15) = 1, and checks at the end confirm that both original equations hold for the found values.
points: Reverse table facts: sin theta = 1 gives theta = 90, sin theta = 1/2 gives theta = 30, cos theta = 1/2 gives theta = 60, tan theta = 1 gives theta = 45, tan theta = sqrt(3) gives theta = 60, tan theta = 1/sqrt(3) gives theta = 30.
Worked pair: sin (A + B) = 1 and sin (A - B) = 1/2 give A + B = 90 and A - B = 30, hence A = 60 degrees and B = 30 degrees.
Worked pair: tan (A + B) = sqrt(3) and tan (A - B) = 1/sqrt(3) give A + B = 60 and A - B = 30, hence A = 45 degrees and B = 15 degrees.
Range discipline: the condition 0 degrees less than B less than A less than 90 degrees ensures A + B and A - B land in the table range and selects the unique answers.
Single equation example: if 2 sin A = 1 with A acute, then sin A = 1/2 and A = 30 degrees, so sec A = 2/sqrt(3).
Shifted angle example: tan (A + 15) = 1 gives A + 15 = 45, hence A = 30 degrees.
Always finish by substituting the found angles into both given equations to verify, since a wrong standard angle fails at least one check.
Common error: reading sin theta = 1 as theta = 45; memorise that sin reaches its maximum 1 only at 90 degrees in this range.

keyTerms.meaning: Two trigonometric facts that translate into two linear equations in A and B, solved together.
The stated bounds on A and B that make the standard angle choice unique.
Substituting the found angles back into the original equations to confirm both hold.

sections.trick: TRANSLATE, THEN ADD AND SUBTRACT: turn each trig fact into an angle equation, add the two equations to kill B, subtract them to kill A.
sections.examPointer: Find A and B from sin (A + B) and sin (A - B) style data is a recurring 3 to 5 marker; writing the reverse-table step explicitly is what secures the first mark.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Exam Traps
sections.para: Most marks in trigonometry are lost to a short list of preventable errors rather than to hard mathematics. The deadliest are reciprocal confusion, squaring the angle instead of the ratio, treating sin (90 - A) as a difference, quoting tan 90 as a number, and solving identities like equations by cross-multiplication. Another family of traps lives in evaluation questions, where students simplify before substituting or drop the common denominator. A third family appears in proofs, where both sides are manipulated simultaneously or where a factorisation like 1 - sin^2 A is missed. Studying this list once before every test is the cheapest marks available in the entire paper, because each item below has historically cost candidates whole steps in otherwise correct solutions.
points: Reciprocal confusion: cosec A pairs with sin A and sec A pairs with cos A; writing cosec A = 1/cos A is an automatic zero for that step.
Squaring trap: sin^2 30 means (sin 30)^2 = 1/4, never sin(30^2); the angle is never squared.
Bracket trap: sin (90 - A) = cos A as one symbol, not 1 - sin A; convert the whole angle first.
Undefined trap: tan 90 and sec 90 are not defined because cos 90 = 0; they are never written as a value.
Equation trap: never cross-multiply in a proof; identities are proved by reducing one side to the other, not by solving.
Missing identity credit: name each identity used, for example using 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A, because unnamed steps lose method marks.
Fraction slip in evaluation: combine terms over one common denominator and recheck the LCM, since 5/4 + 1/2 - 4/3 style sums are where arithmetic errors cluster.
Rough sketch absence: attempting ratio questions without a labelled triangle invites perpendicular-base swaps that silently invert answers.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistake caused by habit rather than lack of knowledge, avoidable by checklist revision.
Marks awarded for correct named steps and identities, independent of the final answer.
A solving technique legitimate in equations but not allowed in identity proofs.

sections.trick: Run the REC checklist before submitting: Reciprocals right, Exact squares on ratios, Complement brackets converted, Equation moves avoided.
sections.examPointer: Examiner reports repeatedly list reciprocal swaps and tan 90 errors as the top traps; one minute spent on this checklist typically saves 2 to 3 marks per paper.

mcqs.question: If cos A = 4/5, then tan A equals
mcqs.explanation: cos A = 4/5 gives base 4 and hypotenuse 5, so perpendicular = sqrt(25 - 16) = 3 and tan A = 3/4.

mcqs.question: The value of tan 1 x tan 2 x tan 3 x ... x tan 89 is
mcqs.explanation: Pair tan k with tan (90 - k) = cot k; each pair multiplies to 1, so the product of all 89 factors is 1.

mcqs.question: If sin A + sin^2 A = 1, then cos^2 A + cos^4 A equals
mcqs.explanation: From sin A + sin^2 A = 1 we get sin^2 A = 1 - sin A, so cos^2 A = sin A and cos^4 A = sin^2 A; the sum is sin A + sin^2 A = 1.

mcqs.question: sec (90 - A) is equal to
mcqs.explanation: The complement of an angle swaps sec with its partner cosec, so sec (90 - A) = cosec A.

mcqs.question: The value of (sin 30 + cos 30) - (sin 60 + cos 60) is
mcqs.explanation: sin 30 + cos 30 = 1/2 + sqrt(3)/2 and sin 60 + cos 60 = sqrt(3)/2 + 1/2; the two sums are identical, so the difference is 0.

mcqs.question: If tan A = cot B, then A + B equals
mcqs.explanation: cot B = tan (90 - B), so tan A = tan (90 - B) gives A = 90 - B, that is A + B = 90 degrees.

mcqs.question: The value of cos 0 x cos 1 x cos 2 x ... x cos 90 is
mcqs.explanation: The factor cos 90 = 0 appears in the product, so the entire product is 0 regardless of the other factors.

mcqs.question: (1 + tan^2 A) cos^2 A equals
mcqs.explanation: 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A, so the expression is sec^2 A cos^2 A = (1/cos^2 A) x cos^2 A = 1.

mcqs.question: If 3 cot A = 4, then sin A equals
mcqs.explanation: cot A = 4/3 gives tan A = 3/4, so the sides are 3, 4, 5 and sin A = 3/5.

mcqs.question: The value of sin 25 cos 65 + cos 25 sin 65 is
mcqs.explanation: Using complements, sin 25 = cos 65 and cos 25 = sin 65, so the expression is cos^2 65 + sin^2 65 = 1.

mcqs.question: The value of 2 tan 30 / (1 + tan^2 30) is
mcqs.explanation: 2(1/sqrt(3))/(4/3) = (2/sqrt(3)) x (3/4) = 3/(2 sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/2, which equals sin 60.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is true for every admissible angle A?
mcqs.explanation: Only sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 is a universal identity; the others contradict sec^2 A - tan^2 A = 1 and cosec^2 A - cot^2 A = 1, and sin A + cos A = 1 holds only for A = 0 or 90 degrees.

mcqs.question: If sin (A + 20) = cos (A - 10), where A is acute, then A equals
mcqs.explanation: sin X = cos Y when X + Y = 90, so (A + 20) + (A - 10) = 90, giving 2A = 80 and A = 40 degrees.

mcqs.question: The value of cosec^2 57 - sec^2 33 is
mcqs.explanation: sec 33 = cosec (90 - 33) = cosec 57, so the expression is cosec^2 57 - cosec^2 57 = 0.

mcqs.question: If sin A = 1/2 and A is acute, then cot A - tan A equals
mcqs.explanation: A = 30 degrees, so cot A - tan A = sqrt(3) - 1/sqrt(3) = (3 - 1)/sqrt(3) = 2/sqrt(3).

mcqs.question: If tan A = n tan B and sin A = m sin B, then cos^2 A equals
mcqs.explanation: Eliminating sin B between the two conditions gives cos^2 A = (m^2 - 1)/(n^2 - 1); substituting numbers such as m = 3/5, n = 3/4 confirms it.

mcqs.question: (tan A + cot A)^2 - (tan A - cot A)^2 equals
mcqs.explanation: The difference of squares is 4 tan A cot A = 4 x 1 = 4, since tan A and cot A are reciprocals.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that (cosec A - sin A)(sec A - cos A) = 1/(tan A + cot A).
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Take LHS = (cosec A - sin A)(sec A - cos A). 2) Convert to sin and cos: cosec A - sin A = (1 - sin^2 A)/sin A = cos^2 A/sin A, and sec A - cos A = (1 - cos^2 A)/cos A = sin^2 A/cos A. 3) Multiply: LHS = (cos^2 A/sin A) x (sin^2 A/cos A) = sin A cos A. 4) Now RHS = 1/(tan A + cot A) = 1/(sin A/cos A + cos A/sin A) = 1/((sin^2 A + cos^2 A)/(sin A cos A)) = 1/(1/(sin A cos A)) = sin A cos A. 5) Both sides equal sin A cos A, hence (cosec A - sin A)(sec A - cos A) = 1/(tan A + cot A). 6) Numerical check at A = 30: LHS = (2 - 1/2)(2/sqrt(3) - sqrt(3)/2) = (3/2)(1/(2 sqrt(3))) = 3/(4 sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/4, and RHS = 1/(1/sqrt(3) + sqrt(3)) = 1/(4/sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/4. Both agree, so the identity holds.

boardQuestions.question: Evaluate: (sin^2 63 + sin^2 27)/(cos^2 17 + cos^2 73) + sin^2 25 + sin^2 65.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Numerator: sin 63 = cos (90 - 63) = cos 27, so sin^2 63 + sin^2 27 = cos^2 27 + sin^2 27 = 1. 2) Denominator: cos 17 = sin (90 - 17) = sin 73, so cos^2 17 + cos^2 73 = sin^2 73 + cos^2 73 = 1. 3) The fraction equals 1/1 = 1. 4) Last terms: sin 65 = cos (90 - 65) = cos 25, so sin^2 25 + sin^2 65 = sin^2 25 + cos^2 25 = 1. 5) Total value = 1 + 1 = 2. 6) Hence the expression evaluates to 2, using only the complementary angle swaps and the identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sqrt((1 + sin A)/(1 - sin A)) = sec A + tan A, where A is an acute angle.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Take LHS = sqrt((1 + sin A)/(1 - sin A)). 2) Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by (1 + sin A): LHS = sqrt(((1 + sin A)(1 + sin A))/((1 - sin A)(1 + sin A))) = sqrt((1 + sin A)^2/(1 - sin^2 A)). 3) Use the identity 1 - sin^2 A = cos^2 A: LHS = sqrt((1 + sin A)^2/cos^2 A) = (1 + sin A)/cos A, which is valid since A is acute so 1 + sin A is positive and cos A is positive. 4) Split the fraction: (1 + sin A)/cos A = 1/cos A + sin A/cos A = sec A + tan A = RHS. 5) Numerical check at A = 30: LHS = sqrt((1 + 1/2)/(1 - 1/2)) = sqrt(3) approximately 1.732, and RHS = 2/sqrt(3) + 1/sqrt(3) = 3/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3). Hence proved.

boardQuestions.question: If tan A = 5/12, find the value of (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A).
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Simplify first: (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A) = 1 - sin^2 A = cos^2 A, so only cos A is needed. 2) From tan A = 5/12, take perpendicular 5 and base 12. 3) Hypotenuse = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13. 4) Therefore cos A = base/hypotenuse = 12/13. 5) The required value = cos^2 A = (12/13)^2 = 144/169. 6) Hence (1 - sin A)(1 + sin A) = 144/169.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that (1 + cot A - cosec A)(1 + tan A + sec A) = 2.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Convert the first bracket to sin and cos: 1 + cot A - cosec A = 1 + cos A/sin A - 1/sin A = (sin A + cos A - 1)/sin A. 2) Convert the second bracket: 1 + tan A + sec A = 1 + sin A/cos A + 1/cos A = (cos A + sin A + 1)/cos A. 3) Multiply the two brackets: LHS = ((sin A + cos A - 1)(sin A + cos A + 1))/(sin A cos A). 4) The numerator is a difference of squares: ((sin A + cos A)^2 - 1^2) = sin^2 A + 2 sin A cos A + cos^2 A - 1. 5) Use sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1: the numerator becomes 1 + 2 sin A cos A - 1 = 2 sin A cos A. 6) Hence LHS = (2 sin A cos A)/(sin A cos A) = 2 = RHS. 7) Numerical check at A = 45: each bracket equals 1 + 1 - sqrt(2) + ... directly (1 + 1 - 1/sqrt(2)) (1 + 1 + sqrt(2))? Computing with sqrt(2) approximately 1.414: first bracket = 2 - 1.414 = 0.586, second = 2 + 1.414 = 3.414, product approximately 2.0. Hence proved.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that (sin A - 2 sin^3 A)/(2 cos^3 A - cos A) = tan A.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Factor the numerator: sin A - 2 sin^3 A = sin A(1 - 2 sin^2 A). 2) Factor the denominator: 2 cos^3 A - cos A = cos A(2 cos^2 A - 1). 3) Express both bracketed factors using sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1: 1 - 2 sin^2 A = (sin^2 A + cos^2 A) - 2 sin^2 A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A. 4) Similarly 2 cos^2 A - 1 = 2 cos^2 A - (sin^2 A + cos^2 A) = cos^2 A - sin^2 A. 5) So LHS = sin A(cos^2 A - sin^2 A)/(cos A(cos^2 A - sin^2 A)). 6) Cancel the common non-zero factor (cos^2 A - sin^2 A): LHS = sin A/cos A = tan A = RHS. 7) Numerical check at A = 30: numerator = 1/2 - 2(1/8) = 1/4; denominator = 2(3 sqrt(3)/8) - sqrt(3)/2 = (3 sqrt(3)/4 - 2 sqrt(3)/4) = sqrt(3)/4; the quotient = (1/4)/(sqrt(3)/4) = 1/sqrt(3) = tan 30. Hence proved.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that tan^2 A - sin^2 A = tan^2 A sin^2 A.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Take LHS = tan^2 A - sin^2 A and write tan^2 A = sin^2 A/cos^2 A. 2) LHS = sin^2 A/cos^2 A - sin^2 A = sin^2 A(1/cos^2 A - 1). 3) The bracket simplifies: 1/cos^2 A - 1 = (1 - cos^2 A)/cos^2 A = sin^2 A/cos^2 A = tan^2 A. 4) Therefore LHS = sin^2 A tan^2 A = RHS. 5) Numerical check at A = 45: LHS = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2 and RHS = 1 x 1/2 = 1/2. Hence proved.

boardQuestions.question: If 3 cot A = 4, evaluate (4 sin A - cos A)/(4 cos A + sin A).
boardQuestions.answer: 1) From 3 cot A = 4 we get cot A = 4/3, so tan A = 3/4. 2) Take perpendicular 3 and base 4; hypotenuse = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. 3) So sin A = 3/5 and cos A = 4/5. 4) Substitute in the numerator: 4 sin A - cos A = 4(3/5) - 4/5 = 12/5 - 4/5 = 8/5. 5) Substitute in the denominator: 4 cos A + sin A = 4(4/5) + 3/5 = 16/5 + 3/5 = 19/5. 6) The required value = (8/5)/(19/5) = 8/19. 7) Hence (4 sin A - cos A)/(4 cos A + sin A) = 8/19.

boardQuestions.question: Read the source and answer the questions: In a mathematics laboratory activity, students cut a right triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and mark the angle A opposite the 3 cm side. (a) Write the values of sin A, cos A and tan A. (b) Verify the identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 for this triangle. (c) Write cosec A, sec A and cot A. (d) Verify that 1 + tan^2 A = sec^2 A.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) For angle A, the perpendicular is 3 cm, the base is 4 cm and the hypotenuse is 5 cm. 2) (a) sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4. 3) (b) sin^2 A + cos^2 A = (3/5)^2 + (4/5)^2 = 9/25 + 16/25 = 25/25 = 1, so the identity is verified. 4) (c) cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4, cot A = 4/3, each being the reciprocal of sin A, cos A and tan A respectively. 5) (d) 1 + tan^2 A = 1 + (3/4)^2 = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, and sec^2 A = (5/4)^2 = 25/16; the two are equal, verifying the second identity. 6) Conclusion: the 3-4-5 triangle reproduces all three fundamental identities numerically, showing that the identities are restatements of the Pythagoras theorem 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2.
